messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Haddad was 41 when he came to treatment, a married man who had built a life in the United States as a professional dancer after years of living as a civilian in a war zone. In the first meetings he spoke carefully, almost flatly, about the event that still seemed to sit just beneath the surface of ordinary moments. During the war, he had been outside near his family’s building when shelling began without warning. He remembered the concussive force of it first as sound—an explosive crack, then a scatter of smaller impacts and shouting that seemed to come from every direction at once. Dust and dirt were thrown into the air. He could still picture the ground torn open and smell the raw, heavy odor of disturbed soil settling over everything. In the confusion, he heard people calling out names, trying to locate relatives and neighbors over the noise. One of those names, repeated again and again in panic, had stayed with him in a way he could not explain except to say that hearing it now made his whole body tense before he even knew why.

In the weeks afterward, Omar did what everyone around him was doing—he kept moving, kept surviving, kept his attention on what had to be done next. But he noticed that certain moments pierced through whatever distance he tried to keep from the memory. A sudden cluster of loud sounds, especially if they had the sharpness or rhythm of impacts, could bring him back to that street with an immediacy he found hard to describe. The smell of soil after landscaping, rain, or even a city park on a warm day could stop him mid-step. And hearing certain names, especially spoken loudly across a room, produced an instant feeling of dread that made no sense to people around him but felt entirely sensible to him. Those names had once been tied to terror and frantic searching; now they seemed to carry the same charge wherever he encountered them.

Over time, what unsettled him most was not only that these moments happened, but what he had come to believe about himself in their aftermath. He often said he felt dead inside. Even when he was performing—doing work that depended on expression, presence, and the communication of feeling through movement—he was aware of a blankness that frightened him. Colleagues praised his discipline, but to Omar it often felt like he was reproducing emotion rather than experiencing it. At home, his wife would ask what he was thinking, and he would tell her, truthfully, “nothing,” because that empty interior felt more accurate than sadness or fear. He had also lost faith in people, life, and anything larger that was supposed to give suffering meaning. Before the war he had believed there was some order beneath events, some decency people would return to; now he was certain that safety and goodness could vanish in an instant, and he no longer trusted promises about how the world worked.

He became increasingly preoccupied with the sense that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. In rehearsals, if another dancer glanced at him after a loud noise in the studio hallway, Omar was sure his reaction had exposed him. If someone’s face softened in concern, he took it as confirmation that the war was written all over him. He began positioning himself at the edges of the room and avoiding conversation after class. When the company rehearsed in an older building with a basement-level studio that smelled faintly of damp earth, he found excuses to arrive late or wait outside until the last possible minute. If someone in the ensemble shared one of the names that reminded him of the war, he avoided using it, substituting “brother” or “man” rather than risk hearing or saying it too directly. These habits cost him. A choreographer recently told him he seemed distant and difficult to read, and at home his wife had grown hurt and confused by how often he withdrew into silence after what looked, to her, like ordinary parts of the day.

What finally brought Omar in was not a single dramatic incident but the accumulation of these moments in a life that had become narrower and stranger to him. A few weeks before seeking help, he was in rehearsal when a burst of noise from a construction site outside the studio made him freeze. Later, leaving the building, he caught the smell of freshly turned soil from a tree bed on the sidewalk and had to stop walking. He made it home, but when his wife asked what was wrong, he could not explain it except to say he felt absent, as if there were less and less of him available to either of them. He came to treatment worried that this deadness was becoming permanent and that other people could already see it more clearly than he could. At the same time, he still hoped for something modest but deeply important: to be in a room, hear a sound, catch a smell, hear a name, and remain in the present with the people he loved.
